html:
The Silver Pavilion, a Zen temple at the foot of the eastern hills, Higashiyama, of Kyoto. Its official name is Jishō-ji. It began as the retirement villa of the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa, who made plans for it as early as 1460. In 1474 he had stones and pine trees taken for it from palaces wrecked in the Ōnin War, and work on its main building, the two-storey Kannon hall, began in 1482. He modelled the hall on the Golden Pavilion built by his grandfather Ashikaga Yoshimitsu. Yoshimasa became a Zen monk in 1485, and after his death in 1490 the villa became a temple of Rinzai Zen, named after him.

The hall was never covered in silver. Yoshimasa meant to coat it with silver foil, but the work was put off until he died, and the name "Silver Pavilion" dates only from the Edo period. The hall today looks much as he last saw it, plain dark wood beside a pond, and its unfinished look is often taken as an example of wabi-sabi. Its rooms were planned around the setting: one corner opens toward the pond and the moon rising over the hills. Around it lie moss gardens, said to be designed by the painter monk Sōami, and a garden of raked sand with a carefully shaped cone said to stand for Mount Fuji.

Under Yoshimasa, the eighth shogun of the Ashikaga shogunate, the Ōnin War left much of Kyoto in ashes. Yet his patronage also brought a new flowering of traditional arts, known as Higashiyama culture after the hills of this retreat. The restoration begun in 2008 kept the old finish and added no silver. The temple is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
